bib.title: Chapter 13: Policy Gradient Methods (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.)

question: How can a policy be learned directly by gradient ascent on a performance measure, with or without a learned value function?
contributions: Policy gradient theorem for episodic and continuing cases
REINFORCE, REINFORCE with baseline, one-step and trace-based actor-critic
Gaussian policy parameterization for continuous actions

results.claim: Policy gradient theorem: the gradient of performance is proportional to a state-weighted sum of q times grad pi, with no derivative of the state distribution.
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.2

results.claim: In the episodic case the proportionality constant is the average episode length; in the continuing case it is 1 (equality).
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.2

results.claim: REINFORCE update: theta += alpha * G_t * grad pi(A_t|S_t) / pi(A_t|S_t), equivalently alpha*gamma^t*G*grad ln pi in the boxed algorithm.
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.3

results.claim: REINFORCE is unbiased in expectation but may have high variance and learn slowly.
results.quote:
as a Monte Carlo method REINFORCE
may be of high variance and thus produce slow learning.
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.3

results.claim: A baseline b(s) that does not vary with a leaves the expected update unchanged but can greatly reduce variance; sum_a b(s) grad pi = 0.
results.setup: Eq 13.10-13.11; baseline may be any function of state
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.4

results.claim: Actor-critic uses the one-step return with a learned V as baseline: delta_t = R + gamma V(S') - V(S). The critic adds bias, not because of bootstrapping per se (a Monte Carlo critic is also biased).
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.5

results.claim: On the short-corridor gridworld (Example 13.1) the best stochastic policy picks right with probability about 0.59, value about -11.6.
results.setup: Switched-actions corridor, reward -1 per step, identical features x(s,right)=[1,0], x(s,left)=[0,1]
results.quote: The best probability is about 0.59, which achieves a value of about −11.6.
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) Example 13.1

results.claim: Epsilon-greedy with eps=0.1 is forced to two policies that achieve start-state value of less than -44 and -82.
results.quote:
If " = 0.1, then these two policies achieve a value (at the start state)
of less than −44 and −82, respectively
results.note: Quote may fail due to PDF encoding of epsilon
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) Example 13.1

results.claim: Soft-max in action preferences can approach a deterministic policy, unlike epsilon-greedy; and supports arbitrary action probabilities.
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.1

results.claim: Gaussian policy for continuous actions: mu = theta_mu^T x_mu(s), sigma = exp(theta_sigma^T x_sigma(s)).
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.7

results.claim: Actor-critic methods are sometimes called advantage actor-critic (A2C); the gamma^t factor for discounted episodic problems was first noted by Thomas (2014).
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) remarks

results.claim: Policy gradient methods in continuing problems use average reward and differential return; the theorem keeps the same form.
results.where: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, ch. 13 (printed pp. 321-338) 13.6

results.claim: Figures 13.1/13.2: REINFORCE with baseline learns much faster than plain REINFORCE on the corridor; settings alpha_theta=2^-9, alpha_w=2^-6, averaged over 100 runs, 1000 episodes.
results.setup: Short corridor, v-hat(s,w)=w single component; step sizes read from Fig 13.2 labels, plain REINFORCE alpha 2^-13 best
results.quote: Adding a baseline to REINFORCE can make it learn much faster
results.note: Curves only; no numeric returns in text

limits: Tabular/linear teaching examples only; no deep-RL, PPO, trust region, GAE or LLM material.
Authors say policy-gradient methods are less well understood in some respects than action-value methods.
Step size for the policy is hard to set; depends on reward range and parameterization.
No PPO clip: mentions entropy regularization and natural-gradient only as further developments.
practices: Use a baseline that is a function of state, not of action, to cut variance (13.4).
Learn the baseline with a Monte Carlo update alongside REINFORCE; step size rule of thumb alpha_w = 0.1/E[||grad v-hat||^2] in the linear case (13.4).
Use soft-max in action preferences for discrete actions and exp of a linear function for sigma (13.1, 13.7).
Include the gamma^t factor in discounted episodic algorithms (13.3 remarks).
Use the one-step return as critic target to trade bias for variance, modulated by n-step or lambda (13.5).

terms.definition: All methods that follow this general schema we call policy gradient methods, whether or not they also learn an approximate value function.

Methods that learn approximations to both policy and value functions are often called actor-critic methods, where 'actor' is a reference to the learned policy, and 'critic' refers to the learned value function
grad ln pi(A_t|S_t,theta), the only place the policy parameterization appears in REINFORCE
update that involves all actions: theta += alpha sum_a q-hat(S,a,w) grad pi(a|S,theta)

lineage.note: presentation based primarily on it; introduced the term policy gradient methods
first obtained the policy gradient theorem

code.snippet: theta_{t+1} = theta_t + alpha * G_t * grad pi(A_t|S_t,theta_t) / pi(A_t|S_t,theta_t)
